summary: Titus 2 tells Titus to teach conduct that fits sound doctrine, with instructions for older men, older women, younger wives, younger men, Titus himself, and enslaved people. The chapter then grounds that way of life in the grace of God, which has appeared, trains people in the present age, and points them toward the appearing of Jesus Christ. It closes by telling Titus to speak, exhort, and reprove with authority.
whyItMatters: This chapter is the center of the letter’s link between teaching and visible conduct. It shows how the letter moves from household and community instructions into a concentrated statement about grace, salvation, hope, and good works.

context.author: The opening of Titus names Paul. Traditional Pauline authorship remains defended, while many scholars understand the letter as later writing within the Pauline tradition.
context.audience: Titus, with instructions concerning Christian communities on Crete and conduct within households and the wider community.
context.date: No year is secure. A direct Pauline reading often places it in the 60s CE; later first-century or early second-century dates are also proposed.
context.setting: The letter presents Titus as left on Crete to complete unfinished work and organize local leadership; chapter 2 addresses community conduct shaped by teaching.
context.literaryForm: A letter of delegated instruction, using direct commands, lists of conduct, and a theological explanation of grace and salvation.

outline.heading: Teach what fits sound doctrine
outline.note: Titus is told to speak what belongs with sound doctrine.

outline.heading: Older men and older women
outline.note: Older men are to be marked by self-control and steadiness; older women by reverent behavior and good teaching rather than slander or enslavement to wine.

outline.heading: Younger wives and younger men
outline.note: Older women are to train younger wives in family and household conduct, and Titus is to exhort younger men to be sober minded.

outline.heading: Titus as an example
outline.note: Titus’s own teaching and conduct are to show good works, integrity, seriousness, and speech that gives opponents no valid charge.

outline.heading: Enslaved people and public credibility
outline.note: Enslaved people are instructed to obey their masters and show fidelity so that their conduct may adorn the doctrine of God.

outline.heading: Grace, hope, and Christ’s self-giving
outline.note: The grace of God has appeared, trains believers for life in the present age, and directs them toward the appearing of Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem and purify a people zealous for good works.

outline.heading: Speak with authority
outline.note: Titus is told to say these things, exhort, and reprove with authority.

keyVerses.text: But say the things which fit sound doctrine,
keyVerses.why: This opening command sets the chapter’s frame: Titus’s teaching must match the kind of life the letter calls sound.

keyVerses.text: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all men,
keyVerses.why: This verse begins the theological ground for the chapter’s instructions and shifts from group-specific commands to God’s saving grace.

keyVerses.text: looking for the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ,
keyVerses.why: The chapter’s present instructions are tied to future hope and the appearing of Jesus Christ.

keyVerses.text: who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a people for his own possession, zealous for good works.
keyVerses.why: This verse explains Christ’s self-giving as rescue, purification, belonging, and zeal for good works.

questions.question: What does “sound doctrine” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “sound doctrine” is not treated as an abstract label only. Titus is told to teach what fits it, and the following verses describe conduct among older men, older women, younger wives, younger men, Titus himself, and enslaved people. The chapter connects reliable teaching with a visible pattern of life.

questions.question: Why does the chapter address different groups separately?
questions.answer: The chapter gives instructions to groups by age, sex, role, and social position. It does not explain every detail of those social arrangements, but it does show that the letter expects teaching to take shape in ordinary relationships and public behavior. The repeated concern is that conduct make the message credible rather than open to accusation.

questions.question: Do the instructions to younger wives settle every later debate about women and households?
questions.answer: No. The chapter tells older women to train younger wives in love for husbands and children, sober-mindedness, chastity, work at home, kindness, and subjection to their own husbands. Readers differ over how directly these ancient household instructions should be applied in later settings. The text’s stated concern here is that God’s word not be blasphemed.

questions.question: Why are servants told to be subject to masters?
questions.answer: The servants here are enslaved people within an unequal household order. They are told to obey their masters, avoid answering back, and show honesty and fidelity. The stated purpose is to adorn the doctrine of God through their conduct. The passage assumes slavery rather than challenging the institution; explaining that setting does not make it a moral ideal.

questions.question: What role does Titus’s own example play?
questions.answer: Titus is not only to tell others what to do. He is to show himself an example of good works, with integrity and seriousness in teaching and sound speech that cannot be condemned. His conduct is part of the chapter’s concern for public credibility.

questions.question: How does grace “instruct” people in this chapter?
questions.answer: The chapter says the grace of God has appeared bringing salvation, then describes that grace as instructing “us” to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts. The result named here is life that is sober, righteous, and godly in the present age. Grace is therefore presented not only as rescue but also as training.

questions.question: What is the “blessed hope”?
questions.answer: The chapter identifies the blessed hope with “appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Jesus Christ.” It places the community’s present life between grace that has appeared and glory that is awaited. Readers should notice that the verse gives hope a future orientation, not merely a general optimistic feeling.

questions.question: Does verse 13 call Jesus “our great God and Savior,” or are God and Jesus distinguished?
questions.answer: WEB applies both titles, great God and Savior, to Jesus Christ. In the Greek, one article introduces the linked titles, supporting that reading. Another rendering distinguishes God from Jesus Christ by interpreting the construction differently. The difference concerns the grammar of the linked titles.

questions.question: What does Christ’s self-giving accomplish in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 14 says he gave himself to redeem people from all iniquity and purify a people for his own possession. The result includes zeal for good works. The chapter therefore connects salvation, belonging, purification, and visible action.

glossary.def: Teaching described as sound or healthy; in this chapter it is tied to the conduct Titus is told to teach.
A phrase used for self-controlled, sensible conduct; it appears in instructions for older men, younger wives, and younger men.
People under masters in the household structure assumed by the chapter; the term here refers to enslaved people rather than ordinary modern employees.
The awaited appearing of glory named in verse 13, connected with Jesus Christ.
Visible actions the chapter associates with Titus’s example and with the people Christ purifies for himself.

reviewer: Codex editorial panel (2 Peter, Titus, Nahum)
